name: Date Difference Is Measured In Years
description: An interval between two dates in this database is measured in whole calendar years by subtracting the extracted years, STRFTIME('%Y', later) - STRFTIME('%Y', earlier), and comparing that to a number of years. 'Hadn't undergone a medical examination until at least a year following their initial hospital visit' is therefore STRFTIME('%Y', `Examination Date`) - STRFTIME('%Y', `First Date`) >= 1, and an age is STRFTIME('%Y', <a date>) - STRFTIME('%Y', Birthday). Do not convert to days with JULIANDAY and do not compare against 365; and never use strftime('%J', ...), which is not a valid SQLite specifier and silently returns wrong values. Year extraction on its own compares against a string year such as '1997'. Related phrasings: a year later, years between, how long after, older than 60 at the time of, until at least a year following.
sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.ID) FROM Patient AS T1 INNER JOIN Examination AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID WHERE T1.Admission = '+' AND STRFTIME('%Y', T2.`Examination Date`) - STRFTIME('%Y', T1.`First Date`) >= 1

name: Patient Attributes Join Laboratory On ID
description: Every query over laboratory tests is anchored on Patient: Patient AS T1 INNER JOIN Laboratory AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID. Diagnosis, Birthday, SEX, Admission and `First Date` are Patient columns, and Diagnosis is read from Patient even though Examination has a column of the same name — 'patients with abnormal anti-DNA, list the diseases they are diagnosed with' is Patient INNER JOIN Laboratory. When the question needs an examination-only field as well — `ANA Pattern`, `ANA`, `KCT`, `RVVT`, `LAC`, Thrombosis, Symptoms or the aCL antibodies — do not join Laboratory to Examination and drop Patient. Keep Patient as the anchor and add Examination as a third table on the patient key: FROM Patient AS T1 INNER JOIN Laboratory AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID INNER JOIN Examination AS T3 ON T1.ID = T3.ID. Starting from Laboratory INNER JOIN Examination without Patient is the single most common way these queries go wrong. Laboratory.Date is the test date and `Examination Date` is the examination date. A percentage over these joins is written CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN <condition> THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(<id>) — the * 100 is required, so a bare ratio is wrong.
sql: SELECT DISTINCT T1.Diagnosis FROM Patient AS T1 INNER JOIN Laboratory AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID WHERE T2.DNA >= 8

name: Counting Patients Across A Lab And An Examination Finding
description: A question that puts a laboratory range on one side and an examination finding on the other and then asks 'how many of them' — 'among the patients whose total cholesterol is within the normal range, how many of them have a P pattern observed in the sheet of ANA examination', 'for the patients with a normal range of creatinine phosphokinase, how many of them have a positive measure of degree of coagulation', 'among the patients with a normal blood glucose, how many of them don't have thrombosis' — is counted with plain COUNT(T1.ID) over Patient AS T1 INNER JOIN Laboratory AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID INNER JOIN Examination AS T3 ON T1.ID = T3.ID. Use the plain count, not COUNT(DISTINCT T1.ID), when the laboratory side is total cholesterol `T-CHO`, total bilirubin `T-BIL`, creatinine phosphokinase CPK, blood glucose GLU or Ig G IGG. The lab range and the examination finding both sit in the WHERE clause. Related phrasings: among the patients whose X is over/within the normal range how many of them, for the patients with a normal range of X how many of them.
sql: SELECT COUNT(T1.ID) FROM Patient AS T1 INNER JOIN Laboratory AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID INNER JOIN Examination AS T3 ON T1.ID = T3.ID WHERE T2.`T-CHO` < 250 AND T3.`ANA Pattern` = 'P'

name: Anti Cardiolipin Antibody Is Three Columns
description: What was his or her anti-Cardiolipin antibody concentration status on a given date? The anti-Cardiolipin antibody concentration is recorded as three Examination columns together, `aCL IgA`, `aCL IgG` and `aCL IgM`, so a question about the anti-Cardiolipin antibody status projects all three in that order rather than picking one. These live on Examination and are keyed by `Examination Date`, while the diagnosis date the question gives for the patient is Patient.Description. Identify the patient with a subquery over Patient on Diagnosis and Description, then filter Examination on `Examination Date`, keeping the two dates apart because they mean different things. Related phrasings: anti-Cardiolipin antibody concentration status, aCL, antibody concentration on a date.
sql: SELECT `aCL IgA`, `aCL IgG`, `aCL IgM` FROM Examination WHERE ID IN ( SELECT ID FROM Patient WHERE Diagnosis = 'SLE' AND Description = '1994-02-19' ) AND `Examination Date` = '1993-11-12'

name: Levels Of Proteinuria C-Reactive Protein And Rheumatoid Factor
description: Proteinuria `U-PRO`, C-reactive protein CRP and rheumatoid factor RF are not recorded as plain numbers. The laboratory wrote down whatever the assay produced, so beside ordinary readings these columns hold dipstick grades such as '+1(30)' and '+2(100)', a bare '-' where nothing was detected, results pinned to the end of the scale such as '>=300' and '>=1000', and results under the detection limit written as '<10' or '<0.3'; CRP also carries the plus grades '+', '2+' and '3+'. A range test therefore reads these columns exactly as recorded — write `U-PRO` > 0 AND `U-PRO` < 30, or RF < 20, straight against the column. Do not wrap it in CAST(... AS REAL) or CAST(... AS INTEGER) to make the comparison look numeric: a cast collapses every graded, pinned and below-limit entry to zero, which silently moves those rows from one side of the threshold to the other and returns a different set of patients. The place a cast does belong is on the aggregate, where it exists only to stop integer division, as in CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN <condition> THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(<id>). Related phrasings: proteinuria level higher than normal, normal proteinuria level, C-reactive protein within normal, rheumatoid factor below.
sql: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN T2.`U-PRO` >= 30 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(T1.ID) FROM Patient AS T1 INNER JOIN Laboratory AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID

name: Normal Levels Of Anti-RNP Anti-SM Anti-Scl70 Anti-SSA Anti-SSB And Anti-Centromere
description: The autoantibody panel in Laboratory — RNP anti-ribonuclear protein, SM anti-SM, SC170 anti-scl70, SSA anti-SSA, SSB anti-SSB and CENTROMEA anti-centromere — is not recorded with the plus and minus notation. A negative result is the word 'negative', a borderline result is the string '0', and a positive result is a dilution titre written as a number such as '1', '4', '16', '64' or '256'. Questions and their evidence usually describe these results in the clinical shorthand instead, saying a normal level 'refers to RNP IN (''-'', ''+-'')'. That shorthand matches nothing at all in these columns, so a query written from it returns an empty result rather than a wrong one. Translate as you write: '-' is 'negative' and '+-' is '0', so a normal or negative level of any panel marker is the column IN ('negative', '0'), and a level higher than normal is the column outside that pair. The plus and minus notation is genuine elsewhere and must be left alone there: RA rheumatoid factor stores '-', '+', '+-' and '2+', CRP stores '-', '+' and '2+' alongside its readings, and the Examination coagulation markers KCT, RVVT and LAC store '-' and '+'. Related phrasings: normal level of anti-SSA, normal anti-SSB, normal level of anti-centromere, abnormal anti-ribonuclear protein, anti-SM within normal.
sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.ID) FROM Patient AS T1 INNER JOIN Laboratory AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID WHERE T2.SC170 IN ('negative', '0')

name: Lab Value Normal Range Labels
description: A question asking whether a laboratory value is within its normal range is answered with a CASE label, never with the raw measurement. The thresholds are: `T-CHO` < 250 total cholesterol, ALP < 300 alkaliphophatase, ALB between 3.5 and 5.5 albumin, `T-BIL` < 2.0 total bilirubin, UA > 8.0 for men and > 6.5 for women uric acid. The label casing follows the measure: total cholesterol uses 'Normal' / 'Abnormal', while ALP uses 'normal' / 'abNormal' and ALB uses 'normal' / 'abnormal' in lower case. Project only what the question names — 'state if their albumin is within normal range' wants the label column alone, with no patient ID beside it, whereas 'name the ID ... and is his ALP within normal range' wants the ID and then the label. Related phrasings: within normal range, at the normal level, is his/her ALP normal, state if their albumin is within normal range.
sql: SELECT T1.ID, CASE WHEN T2.ALP < 300 THEN 'normal' ELSE 'abNormal' END FROM Patient AS T1 INNER JOIN Laboratory AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID WHERE T1.Birthday = '1982-04-01'

name: Average Count Per Time Period Requires Float Division
description: A question that asks for an average number of patients per month or per year — 'how many patients on average were tested each month in 1998', 'on average how many lab tests were recorded per month' — divides a COUNT by the number of periods. SQLite performs integer division by default, so COUNT(id) / 12 truncates to zero whenever the count is less than 12. The fix is to wrap COUNT with CAST: CAST(COUNT(id) AS REAL) / 12. The same applies to any fixed denominator — divide by 12 for months in a year, by 4 for quarters, by the actual count of periods when it must be computed with a subquery. The question never says 'float' or 'decimal'; the signal is phrasing such as 'on average per month', 'average number per month', 'how many on average each month'. Do not confuse this with the percentage formula CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(id), which counts a subset and is already covered elsewhere. Related phrasings: on average per month, how many on average each month, average number tested per month, average tests per year.
sql: SELECT CAST(COUNT(T1.ID) AS REAL) / 12 FROM Patient AS T1 INNER JOIN Laboratory AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID WHERE strftime('%Y', T2.Date) = '1998'
